newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Analysts see Stockholm bourse staying near new high.
newsitem.headline: Analysts see Stockholm bourse staying near new high.

text.p: The Stockholm bourse, riding on new highs, could rise further or perhaps lose some ground but there was no sign of a crash, analysts said on Thursday.

"It could chug along as it is going now with interest rates around these levels, but if interest rates rise there is a risk of a five to 10 percent correction," said Nordic strategist Stefan Ortmark from Enskilda Securities.
"As company profits feel stable there is no risk from this side but the danger could come from interest rates."
At 1110 GMT on Thursday the Stockholm general index was 3,199.02, trading 0.3 percent above Wednesday's record close.

Analysts were judging the six month reporting season that is about to get under way by results posted this week by SKF, the world's largest bearings maker, which is seen as a barometer of global industrial activity.

SKF posted a lower profit for the first half, of 1.10 billion crowns against 1.48 billion a year earlier, but said its second quarter saw improving trends both in and outside western Europe, which it expected to continue.
"For two years people have been saying that things will start to pick up soon. Now for the first time we have a company, SKF, saying this is happening," said Ortmark.
Other analysts do not believe the bourse will be hurt by a slight rise in long bond yields as bigger company profits can add to the stream of funds coming onto the market.
"Liquidity is the biggest advantage. Increased flows into funds can continue to drive the bourse up," said an analyst at HSBC James Capel.
Savings in funds hit record levels in the first half of 1997 with share fund investments rising 37 billion crowns, according to the fund companies' association.
"High liquidity and favourable long bond yields can continue to push shares higher," said Christian Diebitsch, Scandinavia analyst at Paribas.
Paribas thought the bourse could rise another four percent by the end of the year but remained neutral on Sweden when looking at it along with the rest of Europe.
Carl Jensen, chief strategist at Aros, forecast the bourse would end the year at its current levels.
"Our basic scenario is that volatility will continue for the rest of the year with a move of 10 percent in either direction," he said.
"But the risk of a correction is high. The market has put itself in a situation where everyone agrees inflation won't rise, growth will continue and the U.S. won't overheat.
"There is a high risk (that something will happen) when there is such consensus if a macro figure suddenly points in the other direction."
Two events that could push rates higher were a hike in rates by the U.S. Federal Reserve and problems with Europe's economic and monetary union (EMU), Jensen said.
A Stockholm-based analyst who did not want to be named was also hesitant about predicting further rises in the bourse, saying it seemed to be fully valued at current levels.
"The potential for the next 12 months is small but I don't think we will see any fall," he said.
He said there was some upward potential for some shares, such as car safety equipment maker Autoliv, media group Kinnevik and vehicle maker Volvo.

Carl Jensen of Aros was more optimistic about some of the small companies, listing health care product group Getinge and drugs group Medivir as buys while putting sell recommendations on telecoms giant Ericsson and airline SAS.
No analysts expected a repeat of the 1987 collapse in the share market when people had invested borrowed money.
"There's a huge difference if you invest the bank's money or your own," Jensen said. "The bank could demand its money back and you could end up in a forced sell situation."
